speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singaporeans have long recognised NTUC Income as a pillar of social support.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is, therefore, understandable that many Singaporeans are concerned about Allianz's plan to buy a majority stake in Income Insurance.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Allow me to, first, address the PQs relating to the social mission and the support given to co-operative societies, or co-ops, in Singapore, in my MCCY capacity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Minister Chee Hong Tat will, then, address questions relating to the regulatory aspects of the Income-Allianz deal in his MAS capacity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, reserve your questions on the social mission for me, and then, later on, for the regulatory aspects for Minister Chee in his subsequent reply.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Co-ops are member-owned business entities that operate on the principles of self-help and mutual assistance.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They address the common economic or social needs of their members or of the wider community.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Some co-ops seek to provide goods and services at affordable prices for the benefit of their members and the community, while others seek to care for and serve the vulnerable within our community.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will continue to support the co-operative movement to ensure that Singaporeans' economic and social needs are met and that these goods and services remain affordable and of good quality.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have done so in a few ways.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, MCCY has amended the Co-operative Societies Act twice within the last seven years, as part of our efforts to update our regulatory requirements to better support co-ops' formation, operations and development.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, I took Parliament through the latest amendment in April 2024, where one of the key amendments was to provide co-ops the flexibility to tap their reserves to pay dividends to their members.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MCCY will continue to review our policies to ensure that they remain relevant and effective for our co-op sector.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Second, MCCY works closely with the industry body, the Singapore National Co-operative Federation (SNCF), to provide resources and training opportunities for our co-ops.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MCCY and SNCF will continue to review the relevance of these training programmes and provide additional ones to our co-op sector to address current and emerging needs, where needed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Third, the Central Co-operative Fund (CCF) has provided various grants to assist co-ops in their development.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These grants are reviewed from time to time to ensure that they remain relevant and useful to co-ops.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: NTUC Income was established in 1970 with the founding premise of providing Singaporeans, especially underserved workers, with essential, affordable insurance.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: At the time, most of our workers, particularly from our Pioneer Generation, were uninsured.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Through NTUC's affiliated unions, Income provided these workers with much-needed insurance protection at an affordable rate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If a social enterprise cannot sustain itself financially and Government subsidy is needed to prop up the entity, then we will have to consider whether such a service ought to be provided by the Government.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Taxpayers must also be prepared to pay their share of taxes to fund the service.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are areas like preschool and skills training where the Government has a framework to provide funding to selected operators to deliver affordable services.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Where such a framework exists, then the Government has appointed social enterprises, like the NTUC First Campus and NTUC Learning Hub, given them funding support and worked through them to provide the services.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The insurance market is very different now, compared to when Income was first established in 1970.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is, now, a very competitive market, with many options available to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Government has also significantly strengthened our social support system.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have MediSave for Singaporeans, MediShield Life offering universal protection against large hospital bills and MediFund as a medical safety net for those with financial difficulties.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We also have a universal retirement annuity scheme with CPF LIFE.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, Income has to operate in this new environment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, the premiums for several of Income's schemes are not the cheapest in the market.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Besides competitive pressures, there are also regulators, like MAS and the Ministry of Health (MOH), who ensure that policyholders' interests are protected.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Minister Chee will cover this in his reply.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The point is that Singaporeans, including lower-income workers, are well-served by our national insurance programmes and our competitive and well-regulated insurance industry.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: All these provide Singaporeans with wider choices and better value in insurance services and products.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: NTUC has explained the reasons for the deal with Allianz.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: NTUC Enterprise has supported Income with capital injections and will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Questions have been raised about the corporatisation exercise.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: What was important was the need to be upfront and transparent about the arrangements and to allow Income's members to decide whether or not to proceed with the corporatisation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And from a regulatory perspective, therefore, RCS is satisfied that due process was followed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But Income was unable to find a willing partner.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Hence, Income assessed that the deal with Allianz provides the best alignment of interests.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I can understand why many Singaporeans are concerned that the partnership with Allianz may impact Income's social objectives.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I have explained, we need to first appreciate that Income, today, operates in a very different competitive and regulatory environment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, NTUC's Secretary-General has put out a statement yesterday, re-affirming NTUC's full commitment to its social mission.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Companies that provide a "social purpose" will not meet this high bar.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, many companies in Singapore will want to do well and to do good at the same time.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It will not be feasible to legislate and prevent ownership changes in all of these companies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Ultimately, the best way to keep prices affordable is to facilitate competition, ensure options for customers and put in place a sound regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And that is what the Government is committed to doing.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Before I take questions, Minister Chee, will you be covering for MAS now?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This has always been ethos and mindsets of the management and board of NTUC entities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, my first question to the Minister of State is with NTUC Enterprise ceding control of Income to a foreign company, how is NTUC Enterprise able to ensure that the acquired company, which will be foreign-owned now, will be able to continue to do good, like what they have always done before.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And if the acquired entity is no longer able to do as much good, will the Government be prepared to step in to plug the gap?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My second question is, in Singapore's context, entities that run as social co-operatives have always been an added and valuable instrument for the Government to do some of the public good, such as helping to stabilise inflation, to manage cost of living and launch more affordable, inclusive products, whether it is healthcare, childcare, groceries or insurance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, my second question is, in the light of this sale of Income and its earlier corporatisation, do social co-operatives still have a role in our society?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I can understand why and, in fact, there have been many questions with regard to if NTUC had only a significant ownership in the proposed deal, whether NTUC and Income Insurance can fulfil its social mission.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think if we take a step back, the reasons why Income has gone into this proposed deal is well laid out.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are realities on the ground – competitive, Government stepping in to provide that social assurance, as well as the capital requirements.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The capital buffers, for example, were under pressure.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And NTUC has stated publicly that Income will uphold this commitment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: NTUC has also stated publicly that NTUC's social mission will not change.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Ultimately, this is something that NTUC, Income and Allianz, if the proposed deal goes through, they will have to decide together, but Income Insurance will have board members, they will have substantial share in this and they will work together with this proposed entity to fulfil that mission.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On Mr Liang Eng Hwa's second question, there are a variety of social enterprises, co-ops, many of which many Members know about.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For NTUC, there will be a huge portfolio of enterprises, be it in insurance, in childcare and eldercare, supermarket, skills' training, many that I have outlined.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The co-op sector, social enterprises continue to play a very, very important role to provide affordable products that particularly those that are vulnerable and are low income will continue to enjoy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think that is not just NTUC, but the whole slew of the co-op sector which we have been supporting.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I have shown how we have been supporting them – with training, with grants and also with tweaks in the Co-operative Societies Act.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We will continue to support them because we value them and we know that they are a huge value to society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have three supplementary questions for Minister of State Alvin Tan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If yes, is there a time limit to their commitment?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If no, would he agree that NTUC or NTUC Enterprise, has no basis to give the assurance that Income's social mission will be continued?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because after all, if you sell a majority stake to a private company, you cannot have that assurance given to Singaporeans for the very long term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My next question is whether the Government actually continues to view NTUC Enterprise and Income as social enterprises or private companies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My third question is, if the Government continues to view NTUC Enterprise and Income as social enterprises, is it not in the interest to intervene in this transaction to ensure that Income continues to be majority-owned by Singaporeans, so that the social mission of Income will not be affected?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, NTUC Enterprise is a co-operative set up by NTUC and affiliated unions, and the Singapore Labour Foundation – which is a Statutory Board of the Ministry of Manpower – has been providing funding to NTUC over the years.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, I want to say that Income's social mission has already evolved.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It only offers two low-cost options right now, and the other products have competitive options and are well- regulated.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But allow me to also, as I answer his questions, take a step back, because he has questions about Allianz's commitment in writing, social enterprise and private companies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But Mdm Deputy Speaker, maybe I can take a step back, to again remind Members here why.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Because the questions have been: "Why sell?", "Why sell to foreign owners?" and "Can NTUC continue to fulfil its social mission?" I think that is the crux of Mr Leong Mun Wai's question.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I think Mr Leong Mun Wai has also expressed that, as well as others who have asked the questions: why is this such an emotive topic?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is an emotive topic because Income is special to all of us.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For many years, since 1970, it is a trusted brand, it is a brand that Singaporeans identify with, it is a brand that Singaporeans trust.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And for many of us, that is our first policy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For example, if you go to National Service, it was your first policy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And that is why this is something which we all care about and care about deeply, and all Members do so.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Can I also just say that because it is something we care about, we all want the best for NTUC Income, we want the best for Singaporean policyholders, we want the best for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But there are different views about this on the ground, there are different views about this in the House and there are also different approaches to how NTUC Enterprise, as well as Income, will have to deal with the realities on the ground.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And so, the question is whether NTUC Enterprise and Income's approach is the right one.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Because that is what the discussions have been publicly – whether NTUC Enterprise and Income's approach is the right one.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Time is the best judge, but let me, again, put it out very clearly, that, number one, Income's capital buffers have been under pressure.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But it cannot do so alone and it cannot do so in perpetuity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, that is one, the financial capital adequacy that is the reality that Income faces.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The second reality is that, both in the private insurance market as well as the public insurance market, the landscape has changed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In the public insurance market, the Government, over time, has stepped in, provided very comprehensive healthcare, comprehensive insurance, and therefore, that it has become more competitive for Income.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the private space, because we have a well-regulated insurance industry, with a whole variety and suite of options for Singaporeans to choose from, Income also finds itself in that competitive space.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These are the rationales which they have articulated and these are the realities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Then, it also begs the question, could Income and NTUC Enterprise then have looked for other funding sources, which is the question on the ground.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They have looked at financial institutions and non-financial institutions, locally and foreign.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They have also tried their very best, as they had mentioned in their statement, and they have said their preference is that they want, ideally, the deal to be majority-owned and, ideally, for it to be locally.
Because right now, these challenges are apparent in the near term and the medium term.
But insurance is a long-tailed business, as the Members would know.
And if you can fulfil your liabilities now, all well and good.
But if you are unable to fulfil your liabilities 50 years down the road, then who picks up the tab?
So, we can have a very good debate about the approaches.
I think this is what we are trying to do.
That is what a judgement call is and that is what I think is already stated clearly.
What NTUC Enterprise, Income Insurance have already stated very, very clearly.
So, I thought that this is very useful for us to put out there, so that all Members are very clear.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think this whole debate today is that we want clarity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What the Minister of State has mentioned is that the social mission of Income is no longer a very important part.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because he mentioned that currently, there are only a few policies with regard to that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Maybe today, the condition of the market, Income does not need to do that much on social mission, but it gives Singaporeans a sense of security that we always have a life insurance company there, protecting us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Just like we seek comfort in the fact that FairPrice is always there.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: FairPrice is no longer the cheapest in Singapore, we know.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But when there is a food crisis, we have FairPrice.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we are also talking about the long term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, so my question is, first of all, does the Government admit that they are only going to concentrate on the capital adequacy of Income and disregard the social mission?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There were quotes by some of our founding leaders.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: He concluded that a bankrupt co-operative will be of no use.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I have already outlined why NTUC had done its homework and really wanted to make it as majority-owned as possible and locally-owned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If Members were to take one step back and look at NTUC, and look at its social mission, many of us here are advisors to NTUC unions, we have worked very closely with them.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I work very closely with my union's Singapore Industrial and Services Employees' Union (SISEU).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I work very closely with the co-ops under SNCF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But let me put to the Member, Mdm Deputy Speaker, NTUC's history.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These are proof points that the social mission remains true.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These are the proof points that in crises and in peace time, NTUC remains true.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Since its founding in 1961, NTUC has protected and uplifted workers' lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: You meet the workers, they will tell you.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We were just there, at the SISEU convention recently.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And since 1969, the Labour Modernist seminar 55 years ago, NTUC has continued to care for workers and families.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: More recently, on the social mission, NTUC has worked to raise wages of our low-wage workers through the Progressive Wage Model – again, a social mission, focused on workers, because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, NTUC has shown time and time and time and time again, since its founding, since NTUC Income's establishment in 1970, that it has continued its social mission and it has continued to, not just talked about it, but fulfilled the social mission.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But it has to be responsible, it has to look long term.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It has looked at its books, it has looked at the external environment and it has done its homework, and that is why it is doing what it is doing now.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And it has made commitments, which I have stated in NTUC's statement and Allianz has also made its statement as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And so, Mdm Deputy Speaker, time will tell whether this approach is right, but if you think about this, it is very clear that all of these things have been lined up quite clearly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have one supplementary question, a somewhat similar question as that asked by the Member Mr Leong.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In terms of co-ops playing a role, it is very significant.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is that, in terms of market failure, issues that have been addressed in the past, I think market failure in the insurance industry in the past, has been addressed somewhat like what Minister of State has mentioned.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, my question is a bit more technical – it is about governance structure of the new entity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the Minister of State can share, whether there is any reassurance beyond what he has mentioned, from Allianz, in terms of commitment, whether there are any control measures from the governance structure, going forward.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: I do see a few hands coming up, but I do want to allow for those who have filed PQs, to be able to ask their questions.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: So, I am going to move on to the next related PQ.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: And then, I will open it up for supplementary questions.
